call-baal.title: How to show Baal
call-baal.body: Narration: "Allied Babylonian tribes called their gods Baal." Two hilltop gods carry this name in the chapter.

opts.label: Striding storm god
opts.note: A bronze statuette with a horned crown, a raised mace and a lightning spear, after the Baal stele from Ugarit.

opts.label: High-place altar
opts.note: A standing stone, a four-horned altar with fire and a sacred pole. No figure at all.

call-moloch.title: The Jewish tribes’ god, narrated as “Moloch”
call-moloch.body: Vivekananda follows a 19th-century theory that linked Moloch and Yahveh. Israelite worship had no cult image, so a bull idol here would misrepresent it and could offend.

opts.label: Ark of the Covenant
opts.note: Aniconic and historically grounded; the Ark went out with the tribes to battle.

opts.label: Victorian bull-headed idol
opts.note: How 1890s readers pictured Moloch (Flaubert’s Salammbô). Dramatic, but historically doubtful.

opts.label: Two stone tablets
opts.note: Clear and respectful, but it says law more than tribal war-god.

call-merodach.title: Baal-Merodach (Marduk of Babylon)
call-merodach.body: Narration: "Baal-Merodach, said the Babylonians, was the greatest."

opts.label: Marduk’s dragon on blue glazed brick
opts.note: The mušḫuššu dragon from the Ishtar Gate: the best-known image tied to Marduk.

opts.label: The ziggurat of Babylon
opts.note: Etemenanki, Marduk’s temple tower. Reads as Babylon more than as a god.

call-yahveh.title: “Moloch-Yahveh”, over all the other Molochs
call-yahveh.body: The lecture’s own name for the god who won out among the Jewish tribes. We keep his words in the lettering and keep the image aniconic.

opts.label: The Ark, crowned
opts.note: Matches the earlier hilltop, so the viewer sees the same tribe rise.

opts.label: The burning bush
opts.note: Strong image, but it belongs to Moses’ call, not to tribal rivalry.

call-swastika.title: The swastika as an auspicious mark
call-swastika.body: It is an everyday Hindu sign of good fortune, drawn on doorways, account books and the kalash. Viewers outside India often read it through its Nazi misuse. Right now the films leave it out.

opts.label: Leave it out
opts.note: No risk of misreading. The kalash and doorways stay without it.

opts.label: Use it in India scenes only
opts.note: On the kalash, thresholds and rangoli, small and in vermilion, as it actually appears.

call-deities.title: How to show Hindu deities and avatars
call-deities.body: Film 1 shows gods only through their emblems. Later films need Rama, Sita, Krishna and the Gopis, Shiva in the poor, Dhruva and Prahlada, Radha and Krishna (Films 4, 13, 21, 23).

opts.label: Emblems and attributes only
opts.note: Trident and Nandi, conch and chakra, bow and arrow, flute and peacock feather. Never wrong, sometimes abstract.

opts.label: Painted figures in an Indian folk manner
opts.note: Original drawings in the spirit of Kalighat pat and Pattachitra, painted in the same watercolour.

opts.label: Traced 1890s oleographs
opts.note: Raja Ravi Varma Press prints, which are public domain and period-correct. Each one needs a download you approve.

call-saints.title: Saints and teachers on screen
call-saints.body: Shankara, Ramanuja, Chaitanya, Nanak, Kabir, Dadu, Buddha, Guru Govind Singh, Ramakrishna (Films 11, 13, 17, 22). Sikh practice is wary of painted likenesses of the Gurus.

opts.label: Trace real photographs where they exist
opts.note: Ramakrishna (1881, 1884) and other 19th-century figures. Each photo needs your yes to download.

opts.label: Emblems for the rest
opts.note: Bodhi tree for the Buddha, a manuscript and staff for Shankara, the Khanda for Guru Govind Singh.

opts.label: Painted portraits for everyone
opts.note: Consistent look, but invented faces for people we have no picture of.

call-science.title: The science parallels
call-science.body: Several chapters set a lecture idea beside a discovery: Lavoisier 1789, Ritter 1801, Helmholtz 1847, Maxwell 1865, Mendeleev 1869, Koch 1882, Copernicus 1543, Newton 1687 (Films 2, 3, 7, 9, 12, 18, 24, 25, 29).

opts.label: A sepia engraving inset
opts.note: A small framed plate, like a 19th-century textbook figure, sits in the mural. The style change signals the change of subject.

opts.label: Same watercolour as everything else
opts.note: The apparatus is painted like any other object, as with the dynamo in Film 1.

call-photos.title: More period photographs to trace
call-photos.body: Candidates: Sri Ramakrishna; Raja Bhaskara Sethupathi of Ramnad; Raja Ajit Singh of Khetri; Sister Nivedita; Belur Math in 1899; Castle Kernan, Madras.

opts.label: Ask me before each download
opts.note: Name, source and size for every file, one at a time.

opts.label: Approve this list from Wikimedia Commons
opts.note: Public-domain files only. I still show you each one before using it.

style-voice.title: One narrator
style-voice.choice: A single voice (Kokoro af_heart, speed 0.92). Quoted lines use the same voice and show as italic captions.
style-voice.why: You asked for one voice, not two.

style-length.title: No time cap
style-length.choice: Each lecture gets the length its content needs.

style-mural.title: One mural per chapter
style-mural.choice: Drawings build left to right; the camera pans panel to panel and pulls back to show the whole mural, then the board wipes clean.

style-paint.title: Watercolour
style-paint.choice: Layered translucent washes on a paper texture, with a light ink line. No cross-hatching.
style-paint.why: You chose watercolour over gouache and flat marker.

style-reveal.title: Outline, then colour
style-reveal.choice: Each object sketches its outline quickly and floods with colour by sweep, bloom or drop, chosen per object.

style-density.title: Dense scenes
style-density.choice: 20 to 50 things from the narration in each panel: places, people, tools, plants, animals, symbols.

style-hand.title: No hand in shot
style-hand.why: Your choice in the mural study.

style-letter.title: Lettering on the board
style-letter.choice: Hand-lettered capitals (Patrick Hand SC) placed in clear space, key words in colour.
style-letter.why: Your choice in the mural study.

style-quote.title: The quote card
style-quote.choice: Closing quotation in italic serif beside the traced portrait on a sky wash.

style-portraits.title: Traced portraits
style-portraits.choice: People are traced from public-domain photographs of the 1890s and painted from their own colour regions.
style-portraits.why: You approved the two 1893 Chicago photographs.

style-sanskrit.title: Sanskrit in Devanagari
style-sanskrit.choice: Sanskrit terms and verses are lettered in Devanagari (Tiro Devanagari Sanskrit), with English beside them.

style-band.title: Temple border in India scenes
style-band.choice: A red-and-gold temple-tower band runs along the top of every India scene. It appears at once, without animating, and joins up from panel to panel like a sari border.
style-band.why: You asked for it drawn instantly.

style-hindu.title: Hindu motifs where India is the subject
style-hindu.choice: Kalash, toran, lamps, bells, rangoli, temple elephants, peacocks, Om, yantra and the rest appear only in India scenes. Greek, Roman, Western and world scenes stay without them.
style-hindu.why: Your note on making India scenes stylistically Hindu.

style-maps.title: Maps for places
style-maps.choice: A chapter that opens on a place starts with a watercolour map and the route.

style-aniconic.title: Aniconic faiths stay aniconic
style-aniconic.choice: Where a tradition forbids images of God, we show its sacred objects (the Ark, the Kaaba), never a figure.
style-aniconic.why: Set with the Gods of the tribes chapter.
